== Problem ==

Andy and Betsy both live in Mathville. Andy leaves Mathville on his bicycle at <imath>1{:}30</imath>, traveling due north at a steady <imath>8</imath> miles per hour. Betsy leaves on her bicycle from the same point at <imath>2{:}30</imath>,  traveling due east at a steady <imath>12</imath> miles per hour. At what time will they be exactly the same distance from their common starting point?

<imath>\textbf{(A) } 3{:}30 \qquad \textbf{(B) } 3{:}45 \qquad \textbf{(C) } 4{:}00 \qquad \textbf{(D) } 4{:}15 \qquad \textbf{(E) } 4{:}30</imath>

== Solution 1 ==
At <imath>2{:}30</imath>, Andy is <imath>8</imath> miles ahead. For every hour that they both travel, Betsy gains <imath>4</imath> miles on Andy. Therefore, it will take her <imath>2</imath> more hours to be the same distance from the starting point as Andy, which occurs at <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(E) } 4{:}30}</imath>.

<imath>8h = 12(h-1)</imath>  
<imath>\Rightarrow 8h = 12h - 12</imath>  
<imath>\Rightarrow 4h = 12</imath>  
<imath>\Rightarrow h = 3</imath>

Since Andy started at <imath>1{:}30</imath>, the catch-up time is <imath>4{:}30</imath>.  
Answer: <imath>\textbf{(E)}</imath>.

Alternatively, from Betsy's perspective:  
<imath>8(h+1) = 12h</imath>  
<imath>\Rightarrow 8h + 8 = 12h</imath>  
<imath>\Rightarrow h = 2</imath>  
Same result: <imath>\textbf{(E) } 4{:}30</imath>.

== Solution 2 (Simplest Version) ==
Andy goes <imath>8</imath> mph, Betsy goes <imath>12</imath> mph.  

We know that Betsy starts 1 hour after Andy, so she will be 8 miles behind.

<imath>12x - 8 = 8x</imath>  

<imath>4x = 8</imath> <imath>\,\rightarrow\,</imath> <imath> x = 2 </imath>

2 hours after Betsy's start time is <imath> \boxed{\text{4:30}} </imath>

-XaberTooth

== Solution 3 ==
Try the answer choices:

At <imath>3{:}30</imath>: Andy <imath>=16</imath>, Betsy <imath>=12</imath>  
At <imath>3{:}45</imath>: Andy <imath>=18</imath>, Betsy <imath>=15</imath>  
At <imath>4{:}00</imath>: Andy <imath>=20</imath>, Betsy <imath>=18</imath>  
At <imath>4{:}15</imath>: Andy <imath>=22</imath>, Betsy <imath>=21</imath>  
At <imath>4{:}30</imath>: Andy <imath>=24</imath>, Betsy <imath>=24</imath>
You can visualize this using a table:

\begin{array}{c|c|c}
\textbf{Time} & \textbf{Andy - 8 mph} & \textbf{Betsy - 12 mph} \\ \hline
3{:}30 & 16 & 12 \\
3{:}45 & 18 & 15 \\
4{:}00 & 20 & 18 \\
4{:}15 & 22 & 21 \\
4{:}30 & 24 & 24
\end{array}

Thus the correct answer is <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(E) } 4{:}30}</imath>.

== Solution 4 ==
Since <imath>\text{lcm}(8,12)=24</imath>, the time for Andy to reach 24 miles is  
<imath>24/8 = 3</imath> hours.

<imath>1{:}30 + 3{:}00 = \boxed{\textbf{(E) } 4{:}30}</imath>.

Note: Alternatively we can find that the time for Betsy to reach <imath>24</imath> miles is <imath>\frac{24}{12} = 2</imath> hours. So we have

<cmath>2{:}30 + 2{:}00 = \boxed{\textbf{(E) } 4{:}30}.</cmath>

~Boywithnuke

== Solution 5 ==
Andy goes <imath>8x</imath> miles, Betsy goes <imath>12(x-1)</imath> miles.  
Set equal:

<imath>8x = 12(x-1)</imath>  
<imath>\Rightarrow x = 3</imath>

Thus the answer is <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(E) } 4{:}30}</imath>.

== Solution 6 ==

Using constant rates:

<cmath>
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
\textbf{Time} & \textbf{Andy} - 8\text{ mph} & \textbf{Betsy} - 12\text{ mph} \\ \hline \hline
1{:}30 - \text{Starting} & 0 \text{ miles} & 0 \text{ miles} \\ \hline
2{:}30 & 8 \text{ miles} & 0 \text{ miles} \\ \hline
3{:}30 & 16 \text{ miles} & 12 \text{ miles} \\ \hline 
4{:}30 & 24 \text{ miles} & 24 \text{ miles}
\end{array}
</cmath>

Thus the answer is <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(E) } 4{:}30}</imath>.

== Solution 7 (Calculus Overkill) ==

Let  
<imath>D_A(t) = 8t</imath>,  
<imath>D_B(t) = 12(t-1)</imath> for <imath>t \ge 1</imath>.

Difference:  
<imath>F(t) = 12(t-1) - 8t = 4t - 12</imath>.

Set <imath>F(t)=0</imath>:  
<imath>4t - 12 = 0</imath>  
<imath>t = 3</imath> hours.

<imath>1{:}30 + 3 = 4{:}30</imath>.

-apex304

==Solution 8 (Easy to understand, fast)(Detailed)==
Let \( t \) denote time in hours measured from 1:30 PM:

\( t := \text{hours after } 1:30 \text{ PM} \).

Thus \( t = 0 \) at 1:30 PM, \( t = 1 \) at 2:30 PM, and the physically relevant domain for both riders having left is \( t \geq 1 \).

Velocity/position (vectorized).
Choose orthonormal basis \( \{ i, j \} \) with \( i \) east and \( j \) north. Define piecewise position vectors \( r_A(t), r_B(t) \in \mathbb{R}^2 \) (for all \( t \geq 0 \)):

\( r_A(t) = 8t \, j = (0, 8t) \),
<cmath>
r_B(t) =
\begin{cases}
(0, 0), & 0 \leq t < 1, \\
12(t - 1) \, i, & t \geq 1,
\end{cases}
= (12 \max\{t - 1, 0\}, 0).
</cmath>

Define scalar distance functions (Euclidean norm / 2-norm):

\( D_A(t) := \| r_A(t) \|_2 = \sqrt{0^2 + (8t)^2} = 8t \),
\( D_B(t) := \| r_B(t) \|_2 = 12 \max\{t - 1, 0\} \).

We seek \( t \) with \( D_A(t) = D_B(t) \) and \( t \geq 1 \). For \( t \geq 1 \) the equality reduces to the linear equation

\( 8t = 12(t - 1) \).

Bring like terms together:

\( 8t = 12t - 12 \implies 12 = 12t - 8t \).

Compute the difference \( 12t - 8t \) digit-by-digit: \( 12t - 8t = (12 - 8)t = 4t \). So

\( 12 = 4t \).

Divide \( 12 \) by \( 4 \) carefully: \( 12 \div 4 = 3 \). Hence

\( t = 3 \).

~N0lan
